headlines.title: 4.3 Earthquake rattles downtown Cloverdale in Sonoma County, no major damage reported
headlines.description: An earthquake rattled downtown Cloverdale in Sonoma County Tuesday night, startling local business owners and residents, though no major damage has been reported. The temblor was reported at 7:40 p.m., with a reported 2.5 magnitude aftershock, according to the United States Geological Survey. Ciro Gonzalez, manager of La Tequila, was in the middle of serving patrons when the shaking started. “I was like helping my customers and the ladies coming in,” Gonzalez said. “I say what’s going on … then we went behind the door because we’re scared.” At the nearby Sawmill Saloon, the tremor was brief but forceful. “I just felt a giant jolt. … It was pretty strong,” Jamie Karuza said. For David and Nikki Baxes of The Ranch at Lake Sonoma, the sudden quake sparked fears of a larger seismic event. “I was reading the article on Japan today,” they noted, expressing concern that the quake could be a “precursor to something much larger.” Despite the scare, the downtown area appears unscathed. Local storefronts, including an art gallery and several restaurants, remained intact, bringing good news to the community that there doesn’t appear to be any major damage. City and county officials have continued to monitor the situation, issuing alerts to keep residents updated. Further information was not immediately available. headlines.title: Teen lifeguard invited to White House after viral Santa Cruz rescue
headlines.description: A teenage lifeguard is drawing national praise — and a White House invitation — after a viral video captured his heroic rescue of a boy in the powerful surf at a Santa Cruz beach. The video, captured Saturday at Seabright State Beach, has been viewed millions of times. It shows the lifeguard racing into the dangerous waves to save a struggling boy. After watching the video, President Trump called the lifeguard a “heroic young man.” The president announced plans to invite the teen, his family, and possibly the rescued boy to the White House to receive a high civilian honor. “It’s the buzz around town and obviously all the hype around the invite to the White House, that’s pretty exciting,” Santa Cruz resident David Buckalew said. “He did a great job and he definitely deserves to be commended and recognized.” The lifeguard works for California State Parks, where officials noted the rescue is exactly what their training prepares them to do. “It’s great to see our lifeguards working. It’s what we train them to do,” said Tyler Leamer, a California State Parks peace officer lifeguard. The incident occurred during an extremely busy weekend for lifeguards with both California State Parks and the Santa Cruz Fire Department. From Friday through Sunday, city lifeguards rescued 29 people from Santa Cruz beaches. “We had that combination of great weather, large crowds, weekend day and that really large swell,” said Anaiis Moise, a marine safety officer with the Santa Cruz Fire Department. “If you saw the video, you saw how many waves that lifeguard had to duck under before there was enough of a lull for him to be able to get him up on the beach.” Officials hope the viral attention also serves as an important reminder to respect the ocean. The National Weather Service has a beach hazards statement in effect, warning of an increased risk of sneaker waves and strong rip currents. “We’re expecting the swell to continue into the end of the week and the beginning of the weekend — we’re going to see those waves still coming through,” Moise said. First responders advise beachgoers to always choose locations with on-duty lifeguards and to not hesitate to speak with them. Lifeguards can advise exactly where it is safest to swim and what specific hazards to watch for before ever stepping into the water.

headlines.title: PG&E faces backlash over rate hike request for $26.6M shareholder reward
headlines.description: PG&E is raising eyebrows after asking for a rate increase on natural gas to fund a $26.6 million shareholder “reward” payment. The utility claims it saved ratepayers money by keeping costs down and that shareholders should be rewarded. But as NBC Bay Area’s Jodi Hernandez reports, the proposal is not sitting well with customers. PG&E notified customers of the requested rate hike, stating it saved consumers $170 million by purchasing the lowest gas prices possible from November 2022 to October 2023. While most of the savings go to consumers, the company believes shareholders deserve a portion. “Under CPUC rules, customers retain the majority of those savings, while shareholders may receive a performance-based incentive when procurement costs are lower than the established market benchmarks,” PG&E said in a statement. If approved, average monthly bills will go up by about 41 cents. When you’re scraping to get by, every penny counts. Sixty-seven-year-old Janice Mercado and her friend, Janice Henry, had plenty to say after learning about the proposed hike. NBC Bay Area caught up with them at their senior knitting club in Antioch, which they noted is one of the few activities they can still afford. “The PG&E rates keep going up and our Social Security doesn’t. So it’s hard to balance the budget here,” Mercado said. “We all have to count our pennies, that’s why we’re here at the senior center activity or social activity that doesn’t cost a fortune.” Mercado questioned why the savings aren’t returned directly to the public. “Why don’t we get the reward?” Mercado asked. “We’ve been paying bills, give it back to the people that are paying the bills, it’s hard for seniors to make our bills.” Henry agreed, pointing to the utility’s troubled history as a point of frustration. “PG&E needs to drop the rates instead of raising the rates. They need to get back to the consumers instead of the big pocket people who already have plenty of money,” Henry said. “It seems like PG&E has been the cause of a lot of the fires, people have lost their lives, their homes, their livelihoods, their families, and we’re the ones paying for what they did wrong. We didn’t fail to check the equipment. We’re paying bills for what they have done.” Mark Toney, executive director of The Utility Reform Network (TURN), called the request outrageous and unfair. Ratepayers are already asked to shoulder the costs when PG&E goes over budget, he said, and shouldn’t have to pay for a shareholder reward when the utility spends less than projected. “Because PG&E thinks they did well and keeping it not too high, they wanna reward just for doing their job. And their job is to keep rates as low as possible,” Toney said. “If they want their shareholders to be rewarded when they underspend, then their shareholders should be held accountable when they overspend. And that’s not what PG&E is asking for.” The California Public Utilities Commission is not expected to make a decision on PG&E’s shareholder reward request until sometime next year.

headlines.title: Inspectors put baggage scales to the test at San Jose airport
headlines.description: Travelers often question whether the scales airlines use to weigh checked bags are accurate. If they aren’t, passengers could end up paying more than they should. To see how the equipment stacks up to scrutiny, reporter Damian Trujillo tagged along on a “scale inspection” today at Mineta San Jose International Airport. “These scales have to be perfectly calibrated,” Trujillo said of the strict standards. “They can’t be a tenth of a pound over or under, or inspectors will shut them down.” Ryan Atwood, an inspector with the county’s Weights and Measures Department, brought his tools to the airport for the operation. He quickly had to red-tag one scale that was two-tenths of a pound off. When Trujillo asked, “Some people might say two-tenths of a pound is nothing. Is it something?” Atwood explained the strict tolerances. “Two-tenths of a pound, it’s really a small tolerance,” Atwood said. “We’re checking from two-tenths all the way to 100 pounds because different airlines have different requirements on when to start charging customers for their bags.” Inspectors noted that airlines must adhere to weight limits on passengers and cargo in order to fly safely. The annual inspection is coordinated with the airport so officials can have repairmen ready in case a scale fails. The scale Atwood red-tagged required some recalibration to bring it back up to code. “It’s important what we’re doing so the consumer gets charged the correct amount when they check their bags, and our airlines so they’re not overweighing their planes,” Atwood said. “Consumer fairness across the board.” Out of 37 scales checked in Terminal B today, inspectors momentarily closed nine of them. Those scales were red-tagged and recalibrated on the spot. Over in Terminal A, one scale was underweighing by one pound—a problem that primarily impacts the airlines. Overall, inspectors said the required recalibrations were relatively minor. Passengers at the airport appreciated the department’s work. “I think it’s great cuz it seems like it varies,” traveler Marlana said. “Like you weigh it at home then you get here and it’s totally different.” “That’s great. Great news,” traveler Will added. “Don’t want to get charged more than I need to, right?” By tonight, all scales at SJC are accurate, with inspectors hoping to at least take that weight off the shoulders of passengers.

headlines.title: 3 men face felony charges after San Francisco shooting leaves 1 critically injured
headlines.description: Three men are facing multiple felony charges after a shooting left a victim with life-threatening injuries, according to the San Francisco Police Department. At approximately 2:58 p.m. Monday, SFPD officers assigned to the Drug Market Agency Coordination Center were patrolling the area of Market and Jones streets when they heard gunshots. Officers searched the area and discovered a victim who had been shot. The suspect had fled the scene on foot. Police rendered aid until medics arrived and transported the victim to a hospital for life-threatening injuries. Through the course of the investigation, police identified three suspects. Officers responded to Waller Street to search for them, and at approximately 5:52 p.m., they observed the suspects exiting an apartment complex in the 100 block. When officers attempted to detain them, the suspects fled. Following a brief foot pursuit, police were able to quickly apprehend them, the department said. Officers developed probable cause to arrest Donovan Redmond Hayes, 22, and Deandre Gippson, 30, both of San Francisco. During the arrest, police located and allegedly seized a loaded firearm and other evidence related to the incident. Investigators subsequently developed probable cause to obtain a search warrant for the residence of one of the suspects. Officers served the warrant at the residence on the 100 block of Waller Street and seized additional evidence related to the shooting. Hayes and Gippson were transported to the San Francisco County Jail, where they were booked on multiple felony charges. Hayes was booked for suspicion of attempted murder, felon in possession of a firearm, carrying a concealed firearm, carrying a loaded firearm in public, felon in possession of ammunition and an Alameda County arrest warrant for violation of petty theft. Gippson was booked for suspicion of felon in possession of ammunition and possession of methamphetamine. At approximately 12:30 p.m. Tuesday, officers located the third suspect on the 5400 block of Third Street. Police developed probable cause and placed 26-year-old Terry Brown into custody. Brown was arrested on suspicion of felony charges of assault upon a person with a firearm, convicted felon in possession of a firearm, carrying a concealed firearm, carrying a loaded firearm in public and probation violation.

headlines.title: 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan takes blame for the crash that left him with a concussion
headlines.description: San Francisco 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan took the blame for the car crash that left him with a concussion and other injuries, saying he took his eyes off the road to reach for his fallen cell phone before hitting another vehicle. Shanahan crashed into a 21-year-old woman driving in the other direction in Palo Alto on July 14 and was left with a concussion, broken ribs, a broken nose and broken left hand and stitches for a large cut above his right eye. Shanahan was briefly hospitalized following the crash and hasn’t been able to coach the team at the start of training camp. The other driver suffered minor injuries and did not need to be hospitalized. Shanahan spoke to a small group of reporters on Tuesday for the first time since the crash to explain what happened from his vantage point and to make clear the crash was his fault. “I was going 20 miles an hour,” Shanahan said. “I was not on my phone, but I dropped my phone, and it was stuck in my seats. It was on my lap, and it slid off, and I went down to look for it, and took my eyes off the road for two seconds, and as I was coming up, the air bags hit me in my face.” Police filed no charges in the crash. Palo Alto police Lt. Nicholas Martinez confirmed Shanahan’s version of the crash was correct and that a mistake in a report transmitted to a state database incorrectly blamed the crash on the other driver. “I can confirm that Kyle Shanahan’s statement that he provided is correct and that he was found at fault for the collision,” Martinez said in a statement Tuesday. “There was a clerical error in the preparation of the report that was transmitted to the state database. We are in the process of correcting that error. It is the officer’s discretion at the scene of the collision as to whether they issue a citation to either party. It is not uncommon for officers to elect to not issue a citation to either party involved in a collision. Neither party in this situation was provided preferential treatment.” Shanahan has been unable to run the team or practice since training camp started on Saturday with assistant Chris Foerster in charge with assistance from coordinators Raheem Morris, Klay Kubiak and Brant Boyer. Shanahan has come out for portions of the first two practices to watch alongside general manager John Lynch. He said he is not bothered by the sunlight but loud noises like the music at practice are still an issue. Shanahan said he has made considerable progress and expects to make a full recovery. The 49ers have said that Shanahan is going through a similar protocol to the one used for players after a concussion and will resume coaching when he is recovered. Shanahan is entering his 10th season as 49ers coach and is one of the most highly regarded coaches in the game for his offensive acumen. San Francisco has made two trips to the Super Bowl under his watch following the 2019 and 2023 seasons and made two additional appearances in the NFC title game in the 2021 and ’22 seasons. Shanahan has a 91-72 record in the regular season and playoffs for the 49ers, ranking third in franchise history in wins behind George Seifert (108) and Bill Walsh (102). The team overcame significant injuries last season to finish 12-5 in the regular season and win a playoff game as Shanahan finished fifth in voting for the AP NFL Coach of the Year. ___ AP NFL: https://apnews.com/NFL

headlines.title: ‘He deserves it!' Santa Cruz lifeguard who saved boy to receive high honor, Trump says
headlines.description: A teenage lifeguard who saved a boy from rough surf in Santa Cruz will be welcomed to the White House to receive recognition for the rescue, President Donald Trump said Tuesday. The dramatic water rescue at Seabright Beach last weekend was caught on video. The footage showed the 16-year-old lifeguard holding onto the boy and keeping his head above water as they were battered by wave after wave. The lifeguard, along with a counterpart, eventually managed to get the boy back on dry ground. “We’re going to bring this heroic young man, and his family, into the White House with, perhaps, the boy he saved, to give him a High Civilian Honor,” Trump said in a post on social media. “Very brave, he deserves it!” Trump’s son Eric said the lifeguard should be presented with the “highest civilian honor.” Witness Scott Vander Dussen said the waves were coming in at a normal cadence and intensity before everything escalated. “It changed in a heartbeat,” he said. “It caught a lot of people off guard. Unfortunately, this young man was overwhelmed and swept out in just a moment’s time.” After being rescued, the boy was evaluated by paramedics before being released to his parents, Vander Dussen said. “I’m glad it ended the way that it did,” he said. “I’m certain that if the lifeguards weren’t there, he wouldn’t have gone home that night.”

headlines.title: Draymond Green agrees to Warriors return on one-year, $27.7M contract, per agent
headlines.description: Draymond Green is back. Green has agreed to return to the Warriors on a one-year, $27.7 million contract, his agent Rich Paul told ESPN’s Shams Charania on Tuesday morning. Earlier this offseason, Green declined his $27.7 million player option to become a free agent and give Golden State flexibility to pursue LeBron James in NBA free agency. But with James choosing the Philadelphia 76ers, the Warriors made sure to secure their guy. In 14 seasons, Green has averaged 8.7 points, 6.8 rebounds and 5.6 assists through 949 games and 794 starts. Green now will play his 15th consecutive season in the Bay, where he’s won four NBA championships and continues to chase a fifth. headlines.title: San Francisco program teaches life skills through boat building
headlines.description: On the waterfront of San Francisco’s Bayview-Hunters Point, where once upon a time generations of people built and maintained ships, a group of young people were building a boat. It was a small wooden row boat, not the giant military ships or wooden scows and sloops that once dotted the shore near India Basin, but it was simultaneously a nod to both the past and the future. The boat making is a program run by the group Rocking the Boat, a Bronx-based organization that teaches young people woodworking skills, camaraderie and problem solving through the age-old craft of boat building. “We use traditional wooden boat building to help teach kids soft skills like communication, goal setting and team work,” Rocking the Boat Executive Director Chris Childers said. The group of students from across San Francisco meet up in a modern building in the recently rebuilt India Basin Park – just steps from an original shipwright cottage built in 1875. The din of work spilled from the workshop, with students shaping oars, hammering boards on the 15-foot wooden boat, or building their own miniature versions to take home. “The kids along the way to getting the boat onto the water learn a whole lot of stuff,” Childers said. “We’re tricking them into learning math, talking to adults.” At the center of all the action was Anton Hottner, an experienced boat builder who is mentoring the young crew. One second he was helping one student arrange a piece of metal for bending, a second later he was tutoring another student on how to measure a beam for a flag pole, and another on how to affix a new board onto the boat’s hull. Hottner spent 20 years building boats in Sausalito before answering the group’s call for an instructor. “Giving kids a chance to touch things, manipulate them with their own hands,” Hottner said. “They can put it out on the water, they can get into it, they can row it.” The group is building a row boat once prolific on San Francisco Bay. The blueprint came from the archives of the National Park Service, which runs the Maritime Museum on the city’s waterfront. Each boat takes about a year to build, with boats built by previous classes used for community rowing days. “This is like so different to me,” said student Maliyah Powell, who lives in Bayview-Hunters Point but before the class had never been down to the shoreline. “I’ve never thought about woodworking or being anywhere near water like this.” The students will learn to craft the oars, build seats and even build a flag pole. There are also ancillary projects. In a corner of the workshop, student Miles Goodman was intently focused on painting a small replica of the larger boat, which he had even bigger plans for. “I just came here to build more small things like this,” Goodman said, holding his boat. “I’ve made a plan to turn this into jewelry boat, so I can hang all my jewelry on it.” Aside from the building, the group will also go on camping trips, swimming lessons and, of course, learning to row. “Being in this program you actually get to experience new things,” Goodman said. “I never went rowing or anything like that.” The nonprofit program, which is free of charge for the students, is teaching the group to use power tools and machinery like drill presses, sanders and others. “Using all these tools I’ve never used before, the saws, the table saws, the power tools,” said student Victor Lopez. “It’s all super cool to me.” The boat building is not only linking students up with industrial skills, it’s also linking them up with the area’s industrial history. Childers said the program brings in young people from other neighborhoods to help them gain a different perspective of Bayview-Hunters Point, which has a gritty reputation. At the same time, students are connecting with the neighborhood’s maritime history. “So we’re showing our kids not just the cool history that happened in the mud but also what that means in context of living here in the Bay Area,” Childers said. Hottner envisions a future project where students will build an even larger boat that was once common in the area. The Maritime Museum also preserved the 1891 schooner Alma, built in Hunters Point by noted boat builder Fred Siemer. “In this area was a hotspot for boat building and boat repair,” Hottner said. “And to honor that tradition we are dreaming to build a scow.” Hottner said even if the students never touched a tool in the program — which is unlikely — just learning to use a measuring tape is a skill they’ll use throughout life. “I think it changes some wiring up there,” Hottner said, gesturing to his head. “That’s very important in this day and age.”

headlines.title: Bay Area braces for weekend heat as fire danger, beach hazards persist
headlines.description: Warm weather will gradually build across the Bay Area this week, with inland communities facing increasing heat and elevated fire weather concerns, and dangerous beach conditions will persist even with cooler temperatures near the coast. In an early Tuesday morning advisory, the National Weather Service said breezy onshore winds will continue each afternoon and evening through the middle of the week, helping keep coastal areas relatively mild while inland temps climb. Moderate HeatRisk is expected to develop across many interior locations beginning Thursday and continue into the weekend. Forecasters said the hottest days are expected on Saturday and Sunday, when interior parts of the North Bay, East Bay and South Bay could see highs in the upper 80s to near 100 degrees. Interior Monterey County is forecast to be even hotter, reaching the 90s to near 110 degrees, with some areas facing major to extreme HeatRisk over the weekend. Fire danger will also remain elevated through midweek across the Diablo Range, Santa Lucia Range and other inland areas because of hot temps, low daytime humidity, breezy afternoon winds and only limited overnight moisture recovery. The weather service urged residents to avoid activities that could spark a wildfire, including leaving campfires unattended or dragging chains behind vehicles. Along California’s Pacific coast, hazardous beach conditions are expected to continue through at least Saturday, with an increased risk of sneaker waves and strong rip currents. Forecasters urged beachgoers to stay off jetties, piers and rocks, remain out of the water if surf becomes dangerous, and never turn their backs on the ocean.

headlines.title: 3 dead in separate weekend collisions near Gilroy
headlines.description: Three people died in separate vehicle crashes over the weekend in Santa Clara County, California Highway Patrol officials said. The first was a 45-year-old woman from Watsonville who was riding a Honda motorcycle on Highway 101 near the Sargent Bridge overcrossing south of Gilroy at about 5:10 p.m. Saturday when she crashed for an unknown reason, according to the CHP. The woman, whose name was not immediately released, died at the scene. The second was a 34-year-old San Jose man who was riding a Harley-Davidson motorcycle when he crashed into a Chevrolet Silverado towing a trailer on State Route 152 near Ferguson Road east of Gilroy at about 2:40 p.m. Saturday, according to the CHP. The man, whose name was not immediately released, died at the scene. The third fatality was a 56-year-old man from Aptos. He was driving a Toyota pickup on Bolsa Road north of Bloomfield Road when it collided head-on with a Ford F150 at about 4:35 p.m. Sunday, according to the CHP. The Toyota driver died at the scene. The Ford driver was arrested for allegedly trying to run from the area on foot, CHP officials said. Anyone with information about any of these fatalities is asked to call the CHP Hollister-Gilroy Area office at 408-427-0700.

headlines.title: Red Cross requests blood donations to address crisis
headlines.description: The American Red Cross has declared an emergency blood shortage this summer for only the second time in the 145-year history of the organization. They issued an urgent request nationwide for donations on Monday, asking people, including Bay Area residents, to book appointments to donate blood soon. All blood types are needed, especially type O blood, which is under limited distribution to hospitals because the nonprofit currently has less than a one-day supply on hand. The Red Cross supplies about 40% of the nation’s blood to hospitals and healthcare facilities for surgeries, cancer treatment, chronic illnesses and traumatic injuries. “If just three more donors gave at each blood drive this summer, we could help the blood supply rebound and ensure hospitals have the blood products they need throughout the remainder of the season,” said Paul Sullivan, a spokesperson for donor services at the Red Cross. The Red Cross said thousands of people have donated since the emergency was announced earlier in July, but donations still aren’t keeping up with hospital demand. Extreme heat, poor air quality and widespread foodborne illnesses are contributing to lower donor turnout this summer, according to the nonprofit. There are many upcoming opportunities to donate blood across Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco and Santa Clara counties. Appointments can be booked using the Blood Donor App, by visiting RedCrossBlood.org or calling 1-800-RED-CROSS. As a thank you, donors who give blood by July 31 will receive a Fandango movie ticket. In August, the Red Cross will instead offer donors a $20 Amazon gift card.
